documents.title: Guidelines for Using Generative AI
documents.summary: Short university-wide guidelines for students, faculty and staff on using generative AI. They require use within existing policies and the Honor Code, protecting data and using reviewed tools, owning and checking output, and disclosing use. Course-level rules are left to faculty.
documents.stance_why: The guidelines set no default for coursework AI use. They bind everyone to existing policy, data review, responsibility for output and disclosure, and ask faculty to "communicate clear expectations to students on using generative AI in their courses", leaving course rules to instructors.

units.why: The preamble says the guidelines will change: "we will update these guidelines as the field progresses". It is a statement that the policy is provisional, so P54 (revisit regularly); it informs rather than binds.
units.anchor: we will update these guidelines as

units.why: The opening sets the purpose and audience of the guidelines: "important ethical considerations and guidelines ... for its students, faculty, and staff". An institution-level preamble stating scope fits P56.
units.anchor: important ethical considerations and guidelines for the use of Generative AI

units.why: "Use AI tools consistent with existing University policies" binds all users to named existing policies (Technology Acquisition, Data Classification, Institutional Data Management), which is P77 (comply with existing policy) and not a stance on AI itself.
units.anchor: Use AI tools consistent with existing University policies
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on actor, phase, modality and type (P77). They differed only on unit_stance (A restrict, B neutral). The sentence "Use AI tools consistent with existing University policies" only points to other policies and sets no limit of its own on AI use, so neutral.

units.why: "Students must abide by the Honor Code" ties student AI use to the existing integrity code without defining misuse. P77 fits (existing policy governs); P36 does not fit because the text never classifies AI misuse as misconduct.
units.anchor: Students must abide by the Honor Code.
units.fit_note: Does not say what AI use the Honor Code covers.

units.why: Faculty are "asked to ... communicate clear expectations to students on using generative AI in their courses", which is a duty to state AI expectations for each course (P09); the decision itself is left to the instructor.
units.anchor: communicate clear expectations to students on using generative AI in their courses
units.fit_note: Does not say the expectations must be in the syllabus; the place is left open. Asks for clear expectations in courses, not specifically a syllabus statement.

units.why: Faculty are "asked to read the Office of Teaching and Learning's resources about AI in the Classroom" before setting expectations. This is faculty learning support (P63) and the request, with "asked", is a soft should.
units.anchor: read the Office of Teaching and Learning’s resources about AI in the Classroom

units.why: The heading "Protect confidential, copyrighted, and personal information" is an imperative on data protection, so P50 (protect personal and confidential data).
units.anchor: Protect confidential, copyrighted, and personal information.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this heading ("Protect confidential, copyrighted, and personal information."). Checked against the source: it is the section's imperative, and the sentences below it explain the risk, so it is a real policy statement. Kept as P50, must, all, during-work.

units.why: "Entering information into AI tools is similar to posting that information on a public website" explains why data protection matters, including that data "could become part of its training data". It is a fact supporting P50, so informs.
units.anchor: Entering information into AI tools is similar to posting that information on a public website.

units.why: Explains that data entered 'could become part of its training data' and be reproduced to outsiders; a privacy and confidentiality fact supporting the data-protection rule.
units.anchor: Any data entered into such tools could become part of its training data
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this sentence ("Any data entered into such tools could become part of its training data"). Coder A covered it inside its single unit on the whole passage. In the source it is a separate sentence giving the specific risk (reproduction to people outside the University) behind the data-protection rule, so it is kept as informs under P50.

units.why: The section heading "Any AI tool used with University information must follow review processes" requires that tools used with University information go through review. This is the review-and-approve rule (P65), addressed to everyone who uses such tools.
units.anchor: Any AI tool used with University information must follow review
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this heading (A: admin, before-course). The source sentence says the AI tool "must follow review processes" and the bullets below apply it to faculty, students and staff who use University information, so the burden is on the user: actor all, phase during-work, as for the conditions unit that follows. Kept as a real rule; P65 fits (review and approval).

units.why: "Faculty, students, and staff may use University information with generative AI tools or services only when" the information is public or the tool has "undergone appropriate internal reviews and contract terms are in place". The condition is that the tool was reviewed and the contract protects data, which is the review-and-approve rule (P65), though data protection is also its purpose.
units.anchor: may use University information with generative AI tools or services only when
units.frag_start: Faculty, students, and staff may use
units.policy: Faculty, students, and staff may use University information with generative AI tools or services only when the information is publicly available (classified as public), or the AI tool or service has undergone appropriate internal reviews and contract terms are in place to protect University data assets.
units.fit_note: Also a data-protection rule: only public information may go into tools that were not reviewed.
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded P50 (protect data, prefer vetted tools) with a fit_note that vetting is a condition, not a preference. Coder B coded P65. The source makes use of University information conditional on public classification or on completed review plus contract terms. That is approval of tools and data sharing, not a preference for vetted tools, so P65 follows; the data-protection aim is kept in fit_note.

units.why: "If you aren't sure, contact the IT help center" tells users who are unsure whether a tool has been reviewed to ask before using it with University information. That is the ask-before-use type (P10); P72 (human help alongside AI) is about support while working with AI, which is not what this line is.
units.anchor: If you aren’t sure, contact the IT help center
units.fit_note: Directs people to IT staff about tool review status, not to the instructor about whether AI is allowed in a course.
units.resolution_why: A coded P72, B coded P10; actor, phase and modality agreed. The source line follows the review conditions and covers the case of not knowing whether the tool qualifies, so the person is to check before use. That is asking before using, with IT as the contact, so P10 with a fit_note.

units.why: Users should be aware of vendor usage policies that "are frequently updated without notice and should be reviewed regularly". P102 (stay informed) fits best; P52 (terms of use) is about ownership of outputs, which is not the point here.
units.anchor: should be reviewed regularly.
units.fit_note: Duty is to follow vendors' policies, not the institution's guidance. Concerns vendor terms of service and lawful use, not general AI developments.

units.why: "Adhere to ethical and legal standards and norms of the disciplines and the University, with regard to data privacy, consent, ownership, and academic integrity" is a general compliance duty (P77) naming law, norms and university standards.
units.anchor: Adhere to ethical and legal standards and norms of the disciplines
units.fit_note: Also lists integrity, privacy, consent and ownership as ethical concerns.

units.why: "You are 100% responsible for the output you use" puts full responsibility for AI output on the user, which is P29 (own what you submit).
units.anchor: You are 100% responsible for the output you use.

units.why: Output "may be biased, inaccurate, completely fabricated" and requires "thorough human review prior to use". That is the verify-output rule (P31).
units.anchor: requiring thorough human review prior to use.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on every code except unit_stance (A neutral, B restrict). Requiring human review of output sets no limit on AI use itself, so neutral.

units.why: Notes output may 'contain copyright-protected or proprietary information', a licensing and IP concern about AI output.
units.anchor: contain copyright-protected or proprietary information
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this clause ("contain copyright-protected or proprietary information"). It is part of the same sentence as the verify rule but names a separate risk, licensing and copyright of output, so it is kept as informs under P52.

units.why: "The use of generative AI for any DU related research, scholarship or work, should be clearly documented and disclosed" requires disclosure of AI use (P24), with a should, and covers research and work, not only coursework.
units.anchor: should be clearly documented and disclosed.
units.frag_start: The use of generative AI for any DU
units.fit_note: Scope is 'research, scholarship or work', not specifically course submissions; no format for the citation is given.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on type P24 but differed on modality (A should, B must). The source says the use "should be clearly documented and disclosed"; the heading "Be transparent and cite usage of AI" is an imperative but the operative sentence is "should", so should.

units.why: Under "When in doubt, reach out", "Work with the IT staff to get connected with the right people ... explore use cases, and mitigate risks" points users to human help when a case is uncertain. That is P72; P10 (ask before using AI) does not fit because it is not about permission to use AI.
units.anchor: Work with the IT staff to get connected with the right people
units.fit_note: Support is IT staff for use cases and risks, not tied to a specific rule.
units.resolution_why: A coded P72, B coded P10; actor, phase and modality agreed. The source sentence is about getting connected with people to help with the project, use cases and risks, not about asking whether something is allowed, so P72 follows. B's topic syllabus-communication was dropped since the line has nothing to do with syllabi.

documents.title: Concerns About Student Use (Artificial Intelligence)
documents.summary: Teaching-center advice for instructors worried about student AI use: discuss integrity, state syllabus expectations, redesign assessment, avoid relying on detectors, and talk with the student first. It includes views from the Writing Center, Career services and a college.
documents.stance_why: The page advises faculty ("Consider syllabus statements indicating whether and how AI tools can be used") and sets no AI rule for students. It refers to "If AI tools are banned in your class", so rules vary by course.

units.why: States the page's aim: AI use should enhance 'rather than detracts from' education, a purpose statement for the guidance.
units.anchor: ensuring that its use enhances, rather than detracts from, the educational experience
units.fit_note: Purpose statement for a guidance page rather than an institution-wide framework.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this purpose sentence ("ensuring that its use enhances, rather than detracts from, the educational experience"). It is the stated aim of the guidance page, a principle of the kind the codebook counts as rationale, so it is kept as informs, P56, with B's fit_note.

units.why: The page advises instructors to "carve out time for robust discussions about academic honesty, integrity, and ethics" at the start of term. It asks instructors to talk with students about the reasons, which is P66.
units.anchor: carve out time for robust discussions about academic honesty, integrity, and ethics
units.frag_start: At the beginning of the quarter
units.fit_note: Discussion is about academic honesty generally, not the AI rules.

units.why: "Make sure they are familiar with the University of Denver Honor Code" asks instructors to make students aware of the Honor Code. Closest is P66 (go beyond listing rules); P78 is student-side duty and does not fit.
units.anchor: Make sure they are familiar with the
units.fit_note: Concerns making students familiar with the Honor Code, not explaining AI rules.

units.why: "Be very clear about your expectations ... Consider syllabus statements indicating whether and how AI tools can be used" recommends putting AI expectations in the syllabus, i.e. P09, as a suggestion with "Consider".
units.anchor: Consider syllabus statements indicating whether and how AI tools can be used.
units.fit_note: Syllabus statement is suggested ('consider'), not required.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on type P09 but differed on phase (A course-start, B before-course). Syllabus statements communicate expectations to students, which the codebook puts in course-start; before-course is course design. Course-start.

units.why: Offers sample policies and 'local examples' and invites faculty to share their own; resources to help instructors write course policy, closest to supporting faculty.
units.anchor: We’ve added a section to our
units.frag_start: We’ve added a section to our
units.policy: OTL has added a section on AI tools with local examples to its Sample Syllabus Statements page.
units.fit_note: Sample statements and sharing, not workshops or consultations.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on type P63, actor, phase and modality. They differed on wording: A left policy null with a weak anchor, B wrote a combined statement that also included the invitation to email statements. The final policy states only the first sentence, which is what the source says and keeps one rule per unit.

units.why: "Provide multiple incentives for active learning ... assess student learning throughout the course ... formative approaches in addition to summative ones" changes assessment structure in response to AI concerns, so P35.
units.anchor: assess student learning throughout the course
units.frag_start: Provide multiple incentives for active learning

units.why: Asking students for an early reflection and low-stakes writing to "get to know your students’ writing styles" gives instructors a baseline for later spotting misuse. P40 (process evidence) is nearest; the text does not name a detection method.
units.anchor: get to know your students’ writing styles.
units.frag_start: As much as is possible given class size
units.fit_note: A baseline of student writing, not a check run on suspected work.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on type P40, actor and modality but differed on phase (A course-start, B during-work). The source suggests an early-quarter reflection, Canvas posts and low-stakes in-class writing to learn writing styles, so the action happens at the start of the term: course-start.

units.why: "Write specific prompts that asks students to synthesize knowledge and make connections ... ChatGPT struggles with details" advises designing assignments that AI handles poorly, i.e. P35.
units.anchor: Write specific prompts that asks students to synthesize knowledge

units.why: "Don’t rely on AI checking software to confirm your suspicions" because such programs are "unreliable". This is the rule not to rely on detectors (P39).
units.anchor: Don’t rely on AI checking software to confirm your suspicions.

units.why: "Instead of assuming the worst and demonizing the student, take the time to have a conversation" tells instructors to talk with the student before acting. That is P57; the good-faith framing touches P68, but P68 is about educative rather than punitive consequences, and this line prescribes no consequence.
units.anchor: Instead of assuming the worst and demonizing the student, take the time
units.fit_note: Also frames the conversation as good faith, not assuming the worst.
units.resolution_why: A coded P57, B coded P68 (with a fit_note saying P57 also fit). The source's instruction is "take the time to have a conversation"; no response or sanction is described, so the type that matches is talking before escalating (P57). The good-faith framing is kept in fit_note.

units.why: Asking the student "about their writing process" and then "the direct question about the use of AI" is a concrete conversation procedure before any decision, so P57.
units.anchor: Ask the student about their writing process

units.why: "Depending on how the student responds, you can decide how to proceed based on your course and/or department/program policies" lets the instructor decide the response using course and department rules. It fits letting each instructor or course set the rule (P04), as a permission ("can decide").
units.anchor: based on your course and/or department/program policies.
units.frag_start: Depending on how the student responds
units.fit_note: Applies to handling suspected misuse, not to whether AI is permitted; refers to course or department policy.
units.resolution_why: A coded P85 (units set their own) with may; B coded P04 with informs. "you can decide" grants discretion, so may. The deciding party is the instructor, using course rules (department/program is an alternative), so P04 fits better than P85, which is about schools or units. Fit_note records the misuse-handling scope.

units.why: Faculty are told to "visit the Student Rights and Responsibilities (SRR) Faculty and Staff Academic Integrity Resources webpage" for DU processes on misconduct. It points to the formal procedure, so P81.
units.anchor: Student Rights and Responsibilities (SRR) Faculty and Staff Academic Integrity Resources
units.fit_note: Points to resources about processes without stating steps.

units.why: If several students may have used AI, "use class time to have a broader discussion about the uses and misuses of AI tools; reiterate your course and department policies". This is explaining and discussing rules with students (P66).
units.anchor: use class time to have a broader discussion about the uses and misuses
units.frag_start: If you suspect that more than one

units.why: Writing Center advises instructors to be 'transparent about how you are asking students to use AI in their writing'; stating the rule clearly for writing.
units.anchor: be transparent about how you are asking students to use AI in their writing
units.frag_start: Our best advice to faculty is to
units.fit_note: Applies to writing assignments; not a syllabus requirement as such.

units.why: The same advice to "be transparent about how you are asking students to use AI" and give "class time to discuss that policy" asks for explaining the rules to students. P66 fits and P09 was used for the written policy.
units.anchor: class time to discuss that policy

units.why: The "before and after" assignment (write, ask AI to edit, compare, "turn all three pieces in") is a redesign around AI that shows process, so P35 (assignment-specific AI protocol).
units.anchor: write a response to a question and save that response
units.frag_start: We’ve seen a few students working on
units.fit_note: Also lets students use AI to edit their writing and submit all versions.

units.why: The Writing Center warns AI "may flatten individual voices, cultural markers, and linguistic diversity" and asks faculty to talk with students about this. This names a harm of AI, so P53.
units.anchor: AI may flatten individual voices, cultural markers, and linguistic diversity
units.frag_start: We’d ask faculty to consider when

units.why: Faculty should "ask students to edit their own work after using AI, including rejecting some of the changes that AI might have made". Students stay in charge of their text, so P32; the "after AI" order is not a ban on early use.
units.anchor: ask students to edit their own work after using AI
units.frag_start: We hope faculty will talk with their students
units.fit_note: Instructor asks for student editing of AI-changed text; also sequences editing after AI.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P32, actor, phase and modality; unit_stance differed (A permit, B neutral). The sentence takes student AI use as given ("edit their own work after using AI") and asks only that students keep control, so the unit permits AI use with that condition: permit.

units.why: Says students 'should be encouraged to have their own voices come through' in writing; keeps the student as author.
units.anchor: they should be encouraged to have their own voices come through in their written work
units.frag_start: There are students who take even
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this sentence ("they should be encouraged to have their own voices come through in their written work"). It is the Writing Center's recommendation that students stay the authors of their writing, which is a real statement; kept as P32 with should.

units.why: Career & Professional Development provides a guide to "using generative AI ... for career exploration, resumes, cover letters, interview preparation, and networking" with sample prompts. This teaches AI use for career tasks, so P44; no restriction.
units.anchor: career exploration, resumes, cover letters, interview preparation, and networking
units.frag_start: It provides students with specific guidance
units.frag_end: sample prompts are provided for each of these topics.
units.fit_note: Career-tasks guidance, outside coursework.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on modality (informs) but differed on actor (A student, B admin), phase (A during-work, B general) and type (A P44, B P70). The passage describes a Career & Professional Development guide that teaches students to use generative AI for career exploration, resumes, cover letters, interviews and networking, with sample prompts. That is teaching effective AI use as a professional skill (P44), a student-facing guide, so actor student and phase during-work. P70 (provide AI training) was rejected because this is a resource, not training.

units.why: The guide "highlights the general concerns ... accuracy and AI hallucinations, ethics, and privacy", telling students to stay aware of them. This is the verify-output theme (P31) with ethics and privacy mentioned.
units.anchor: accuracy and AI hallucinations, ethics, and privacy
units.frag_start: It also highlights the general concerns
units.fit_note: Also names ethics and privacy, not only accuracy.

units.why: The University College of Professional Studies "has introduced two self-paced AI tutorials (one for students and one for instructors)" for AI literacy and clear expectations. Training for students and staff is P70.
units.anchor: two self-paced AI tutorials (one for students and one for instructors)
units.frag_start: As part of a multi-part AI strategic plan
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on actor, modality and type (P70, admin, informs) but differed on phase (A before-course, B general). The tutorials are set up in advance so that everyone has the same knowledge and expectations before courses run: before-course.

notes: Reconciled consensus of Coder A and Coder B. No school or computing-unit documents were collected; course layer deferred. Merged fit_notes from both coders; no UNCOVERED units; no new types.
